title: The scythe
hookLine: in Tolstoy, Levin mows with the peasants and loses himself in the rhythm (Anna Karenina, part 3, 4–5)

cards: Early morning, dew still on the grass. A landowner named Levin has decided to mow his own meadow, shoulder to shoulder with the men who work his land. He is out of practice.
His strokes are clumsy, his back aches, and an old peasant ahead of him moves down the row as if it costs him nothing. Levin is sure he'll have to quit. He doesn't.
Something changes in the middle of the morning, and Tolstoy takes his time showing what it is. Today: the scythe.

teach.h: THE HARDER HE TRIES, THE WORSE.
teach.b: The scene is in Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina, in the third part of the book. First, the struggle. Levin tries hard.
He watches the row, worries how he looks, measures how far is left. And the harder he tries, the worse he mows. Second, the turn.
After a rest, the work goes on, and at some point Levin stops thinking about the stroke.

teach.h: THE SCYTHE MOVES ON ITS OWN.
teach.b: In Tolstoy's telling, there come moments when he forgets himself, and the scythe seems to move on its own, as if the body knew what the mind kept getting in the way of. Those are the moments when his row is straightest.
When he starts thinking about it again, the swing gets worse. Third, the old man.
The peasant ahead never seems to strain. He stops to sharpen his blade, to eat, to drink, to talk. He isn't racing; he's simply inside the work, and the work carries him.
Tolstoy gives him no speech about it. He just mows, and that is the lesson. Fourth, what Levin finds.
By the end of the day he is tired and strangely happy.
Because for a few hours the gap between him and the task closed. Tolstoy doesn't call it prayer or meditation. He only shows it.

Some readers find a spiritual teaching here anyway: that self-forgetting can arrive through the hands, in plain hard work, and that it comes when you stop grabbing for it. Tomorrow, a scientist puts a name to this.

how: Readers of Anna Karenina often come back to the mowing chapters as a picture of absorbed work; some people take up a rhythmic task, like gardening, sweeping or kneading bread, as a quiet practice of self-forgetting.

s: in the scene, Levin mows best when he concentrates hardest on each stroke
it's the reverse: his row is straightest when he forgets himself and stops watching the stroke.
the old peasant stops to sharpen, eat and drink as he works
he isn't racing; he's simply inside the work.
Tolstoy explains the experience as a kind of prayer

games.q: you're Levin. your back aches, your strokes are clumsy, and the old man is far ahead. what do you do?
o: keep going, and somewhere in the work stop thinking about it.
race the old man to prove yourself.
games.why: he keeps going, and in the middle of the morning he forgets himself. the scythe seems to mow on its own, and he ends the day tired and happy.

practice: Let the breath be the swing: in as the blade draws back, out as it sweeps through the grass, or, if you're able, rock gently forward and back, or tap one finger slowly on your knee. Don't count, and don't judge the stroke.
When you catch yourself watching yourself, the way Levin did, let that go and come back to the swing; only the next stroke matters.

wordCard.voice: The scythe. A long curved blade swung through grass, and in Tolstoy's meadow, a picture of work that carries you when you stop forcing it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the scythe moves. The work can carry you. Day nine hundred seven, done.
